notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended November 30, 2024, as the city reported them to the Census Bureau's Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by parish school boards, which are separate governments, so they are not included. Residents also pay Orleans Parish.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
Payments to other governments ($23,564,000) are left out, because the government receiving them reports that spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.

Political money counts contributions from businesses, unions and PACs to candidates for mayor, council or board of aldermen and chief of police, e-filed with the Board of Ethics since 2023. Candidates are matched to the office they typed when filing; reports filed on paper are not included. Louisiana allows business and union contributions. Individuals, candidates' own money, in-kind gifts, and party and candidate committees are not counted.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Cameras: 132 license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of New Orleans's borders in OpenStreetMap (66 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-20. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Louisiana yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: Flock camera network
redFlags.detail: 66 Flock Safety license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of New Orleans's borders in OpenStreetMap. Flock cameras photograph every passing car and feed a search network shared with police agencies across the country. Who runs each camera is not recorded; cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies are not counted.

redFlags.label: Real-time crime center
redFlags.agency: New Orleans Office of Homeland Security
redFlags.detail: The New Orleans Police Department opened its real-time crime center in November 2017 as a part of the $40-million Citywide Public Safety Improvement Plan. As of December 2018, the RTCC employs a staff of 18 and accesses more than 340 cameras. In February 2018, there were plans to spend another $2.5 million on cameras and installation, including 120 automated license plate readers and up to 250 more cameras.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS006559, citing The Lens

redFlags.label: License-plate readers
redFlags.detail: The New Orleans Police Department owned 46 automated license plate readers as of 2017.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS007004, citing The Times Picayune

redFlags.label: Private camera registry
redFlags.detail: The New Orleans Police Department operates a camera registry through its "SafeCam" program.
